nature-gov-159.title: Managing people, not nature
nature-gov-159.text: A forester cannot negotiate with a forest. What foresters, fishery officers and planners actually manage is people: how societies use, change and harm the environment around them. That is environmental resource management. Its goal is to keep ecosystems intact and protect the services nature provides for future generations, weighing ethical, economic and ecological concerns together. The reason is simple. The economy works inside nature and depends on the goods and services that natural ecosystems supply. The field links several older trades, including fisheries, forest and wildlife management. It also takes in the formal systems firms use to track their environmental impact. ISO 14001 is the most widely used standard of this kind. It lines up closely with the EU's Eco-Management and Audit Scheme. Underneath every strategy lies a view of how humans relate to nature. At one end sits anthropocentrism, which values nature only for what it does for people. At the other sits ecocentrism, which grants nature value in itself. Thinking has shifted too. Resilience thinking, which asks how systems absorb shocks, urges managers to stop chasing maximum sustainable yield, the largest harvest that can be taken year after year. It asks them to manage whole ecosystems instead.

nature-nbs-146.title: Adaptive management: learning while you decide
nature-nbs-146.text: Every management decision is also an experiment, whether anyone admits it or not. Adaptive management makes that explicit. It is a structured, repeated way of deciding under uncertainty, described in {{ref:nature-econ-772}}: act, monitor what happens, learn, and adjust. Each decision chases management goals while also gathering information that will improve the next one. The approach was developed by C. J. Walters and his colleague Holling at the University of British Columbia. They split it into two forms. Passive adaptive management values learning only because it leads to better outcomes. Active adaptive management writes learning into the objective itself. Its main features are decisions made in rounds, feedback between monitoring and those decisions, and treating uncertainty as a chance to understand more. In conservation it has three parts: testing assumptions, changing interventions in light of monitoring, and recording lessons. The hard part is balance. Managers must weigh learning for the future against getting the best result now from what they already know. Proving that the method works is also hard. Nobody can watch another approach play out in exactly the same situation.

nature-gov-117.title: Environmental governance: who decides about nature
nature-gov-117.text: In a 2018 study of 461 waterbird species at more than 25,000 sites, one factor stood out. Strong environmental governance was among the most reliable predictors of whether conservation succeeded. Environmental governance is the way decisions get made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources. Governments take part, but so do businesses and civil society. Its key principles include building the environment into every level of decision-making. Cities, economic life and politics are treated as part of the environment, not separate from it. It also pushes a shift from cradle-to-grave systems, where products end as waste, toward cradle-to-cradle systems that loop materials back, such as zero-waste strategies. The obstacles are large. Global agreements are weak, and the UN, governments, business and civil society coordinate poorly. Trade and finance bodies such as the WTO carry more weight than environmental ones. The gap between a human action and its environmental effect can last a generation. Since the 1970s many new international institutions have appeared, which brings overlap and fragmentation but also chances to cooperate. Locally, the emphasis has moved toward community participation and decentralization, a bottom-up break from earlier top-down, state-driven approaches.

nature-gov-141.title: Treaties for the planet: international environmental agreements
nature-gov-141.text: The first one, in 1857, dealt with water flowing from Lake Constance to Austria and Switzerland. By 2012, countries had concluded 747 more like it. An international environmental agreement is a treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources. A deal between two nations is bilateral. One among three or more is a multilateral environmental agreement, or MEA. Their numbers grew after the 1972 Stockholm Conference, whose declaration was the first universal document of importance on an environmental issue. They face a basic weakness. No country can be forced to join, so a nation facing costs may shirk while others comply and still enjoy the benefits. That is the classic free-rider problem, explained in {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Treaty makers have tools against it. Trade sanctions can target non-signatories. Shared funds can spread costs, like the Montreal Protocol's $240 million fund. Differential obligations, as in the Kyoto Protocol, set different targets based mainly on each country's level of development, which can widen participation. Even so, critics call these agreements slow. They say the deals drift toward the lowest common denominator and lack monitoring and enforcement.

nature-gov-148.title: National parks: protected land and its critics
nature-gov-148.text: In 1872 the United States set aside Yellowstone, widely held to be the world's first national park. A national park is government-owned, protected land kept for conservation because of its outstanding natural, historic or cultural value to the nation. The IUCN, a global conservation body, ranks such parks as Category II reserves. Its 1971 criteria included a minimum size of 1,000 hectares and a ban on exploiting natural resources. Many countries use the term loosely. In the UK a national park is a scenic, lightly developed area with planning limits, and it may hold sizeable towns. Parks Canada, set up in 1911, is the world's oldest park service, and Canada has 450,000 km2 of national park space. Parks also draw tourists: in Costa Rica, park tourism rose by 400% from 1985 to 1999. Not everyone celebrates them. Critics say parks in former colonies pushed native communities off their land, a kind of eco-land grabbing. They argue this spreads the idea that nature is protected only where people are absent.

nature-gov-135.title: The European Green Deal and its discontents
nature-gov-135.text: In 2017, more than 75% of the European Union's greenhouse gas emissions came from producing and using energy. The European Green Deal, a package of European Commission policies approved in 2020, aims to make the EU climate neutral by 2050, with net-zero emissions. It reviews every existing law for its climate effects. It adds new laws on the circular economy, building renovation, biodiversity, farming and innovation. Its parts include the Farm to Fork food strategy, a Zero Pollution Action Plan, the EU Biodiversity Strategy and a binding law on restoring nature. A Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism puts carbon tariffs on imports from countries that cut emissions more slowly. A Just Transition Mechanism sends more aid to countries with more coal and oil shale workers or higher emissions. The deal pleases few completely. Environmental groups say it falls short of ending fossil fuels. Some governments, industries and farmers blame it for higher energy prices, lost competitiveness and farmer protests.

nature-gov-152.title: The Rio Declaration: 27 principles for a fair future
nature-gov-152.text: The Rio Declaration fits on a few pages. Produced at the 1992 summit in Rio, described in {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, it sets out 27 principles to guide countries toward sustainable development. Its first principle puts people at the center: they are entitled to healthy, productive lives in balance with nature. Principle 15 states the precautionary principle, to be applied by each state according to its capabilities. Principle 16 encourages the polluter pays principle where it serves the public interest and does not distort trade and investment. Principle 10 stresses citizens' right to take part and to see environmental information, ideas later spelled out in a treaty signed in Aarhus, Denmark. The declaration built on the declaration of the 1972 Stockholm Conference, aiming for principles states could write into their own laws. It raised environmental awareness. Yet evidence from 2007 suggested that little of its environmental goals had been achieved.

nature-gov-127.title: Agenda 21: a global plan with local roots
nature-gov-127.text: In June 1992, 178 governments at the summit in Rio de Janeiro voted to adopt Agenda 21. It is a United Nations action plan for sustainable development, and it binds no one. It has four sections. They cover social and economic issues, managing resources, the role of major groups in society, and the means of putting it into practice. It is meant to work at local, national and global levels. Every local government is expected to write its own local version. Because carrying it out is voluntary, results have varied from country to country. Its ideas lasted. The 2015 global development goals took up its goals and reaffirmed them, in 17 goals. In the United States, the plan also became a target of conspiracy theories that called it a UN plot against property rights and sovereignty.

nature-gov-134.title: Ecosystem management: keeping the whole system working
nature-gov-134.text: American fire suppression shows what goes wrong when one goal rules. Putting out every fire let fuel build up, and later fires burned hotter. Industrial societies often managed nature this way, maximizing the yield of a single resource. Ecosystem management takes the opposite view. It aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs. Indigenous communities practiced it implicitly for millennia. It became a formal concept in the 1990s, and US Forest Service chief F. Dale Robertson formalized the term in 1992. Unlike command-and-control management, which often weakens an ecosystem's resilience, its ability to recover from shocks, it is holistic and adaptive. It treats long-term production of goods and services as a precondition, not an afterthought. It works through adaptive and strategic management, conservation across whole landscapes and broad involvement of the public. The idea is still ambiguous and controversial. Some versions rest on contested claims about policy and science.

nature-gov-137.title: Global governance: rules without a world government
nature-gov-137.text: No world government exists, yet countries still make, monitor and enforce rules together. Global governance is the set of institutions that coordinates behavior across borders. It helps actors cooperate, settles disputes and eases collective action problems, where everyone gains from cooperation but each is tempted to hold back. Power in it is spread out. Intergovernmental bodies, NGOs, businesses and civil society all exercise influence alongside states. Its arrangements can be formal laws and institutions, or informal guidelines, practices and coalitions. The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was one of the first organizations to promote it. Treaty secretariats, like that of the UN climate convention, carry real influence but cannot enforce laws. For sustainability, the system is badly fragmented. A 2022 study counted 335 international organizations in the field, often weakly connected and competing for resources.

nature-gov-116.title: Ecosystem-based management: no park is an island
nature-gov-116.text: In 1979 the Craigheads found that Yellowstone's grizzly bears could not survive inside the park's boundaries alone. Their finding backed an older insight. Back in 1932, an Ecological Society of America committee had argued that US national parks must protect all the ecosystems they contain. Ecosystem-based management grew from such ideas. It weighs every interaction within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of tackling single issues, species or services one at a time. Its roots also run through Great Lakes policy of the late 1970s. The 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement rested on the claim that "no park is an island." Its goals must cover social, cultural and economic values as well as scientific ones, and communities take part throughout. At sea, it means weighing all the human activities that affect marine life together. Since linked human and natural systems cannot be fully predicted, adaptive management is recommended. Scientists now favor this approach for fisheries, though a debate continues over whether it has been fully put into practice.

nature-gov-133.title: The ecosystem approach of the biodiversity convention
nature-gov-133.text: Under the UN's biodiversity treaty, one idea became central in November 1995: the ecosystem approach. It is a framework for managing land, water and living resources together, promoting conservation and fair, sustainable use. It brings people, the economy and ecology into the solution of a given problem. At their fifth meeting, the parties asked their scientific advisory body to describe the approach, and that description came with 12 principles. It has two close relatives, ecosystem management and ecosystem-based management. All three aim to conserve ecosystems but differ in framework and methods. Applied to fishing, it becomes the ecosystem approach to fisheries, which builds a local strategy for each fishery's ecosystem.

nature-gov-149.title: Public participation: a say for those affected
nature-gov-149.text: People affected by a decision have a right to help make it. That is the core of public participation: involving the public, especially those affected or interested, in the decisions of an organization or project. It goes further than stakeholder engagement, because it implies that what the public says can change the outcome. It is a recognized environmental principle, enshrined in the Rio Declaration. Governments cannot solve environmental problems alone, and involving the public can improve transparency, accountability and compliance with environmental law. Taking part is not equally easy for everyone. Low-income citizens often struggle with childcare costs, time off work and limited access to education about public matters. And the hoped-for gain in public trust has yet to be confirmed.

nature-gov-129.title: The Basel Convention and the waste trade
nature-gov-129.text: A ship loaded with incinerator ash from Philadelphia dumped half its cargo on a beach in Haiti. The Khian Sea incident helped trigger the Basel Convention, a treaty limiting movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from rich to poorer ones. The trade had grown because tighter laws in rich countries in the 1970s made disposal costly. Opened for signature on 21 March 1989, the convention entered into force on 5 May 1992 and had 191 parties as of June 2024. It requires notice, consent and tracking for every cross-border shipment. It also aims to deal with waste as close to its source as possible, which rewards producing less. In May 2019 it was amended to cover plastic waste, over the objection of the United States, a non-party. It calls illegal waste traffic criminal, yet contains no enforcement provisions.

nature-gov-124.title: Climate governance: steering the world on climate
nature-gov-124.text: A country that stays out of a climate agreement still gains when others cut their emissions. That free benefit haunts climate governance, the diplomacy and mechanisms meant to steer societies to prevent, slow or adapt to climate change. It rests on three pillars: mitigation, which cuts emissions; adaptation, which copes with change; and the means to carry them out. A milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which hoped to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, each country submits its own pledge, a nationally determined contribution that is not legally binding. A divide runs between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones. It underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Governance works at many scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts acting beside states. It leans increasingly on markets, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, alongside command-and-control rules.

nature-gov-131.title: Taking climate change to court
nature-gov-131.text: In 2021 a court in The Hague ordered Royal Dutch Shell to cut its global carbon emissions by 45% by 2030 from 2019 levels. The order even covered emissions from the products it sells. Climate change litigation uses lawsuits to set legal precedents that push governments and companies to act. It grew because climate politics was slow to deliver emission cuts. Cases usually rest on one of five kinds of claim: constitutional, administrative, private law, fraud or consumer protection, or human rights. They rose from 884 in 24 countries in 2017 to at least 1,550 in 38 countries by July 2020, most in the United States. In the Urgenda case, Dutch courts ordered the government to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by the end of 2020. In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights became the first international court to rule that state inaction on climate violates human rights. Results are mixed. Companies may hit back, as RWE did with a claim against the Netherlands under the Energy Charter Treaty.

nature-gov-126.title: The Aarhus Convention: rights to know, speak and sue
nature-gov-126.text: Signed in Aarhus, Denmark, on 25 June 1998, this UNECE treaty gives the public three environmental rights. People may get environmental information, take part in decisions, and go to court when environmental law is broken. It entered into force on 30 October 2001. By April 2023 it had 49 parties, 48 states plus the European Union, almost all in Europe and Central Asia. It binds public authorities but not private companies, whose disclosure stays voluntary. Its compliance system is unique in international environmental law: members of the public can complain straight to a committee of legal experts. Its Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on pollutant release and transfer registers, inventories of pollution from industry and other sources. Kofi Annan called it the most impressive elaboration of Principle 10 of the Rio Declaration. Critics disagree. They say its focus on procedure makes it vague, that ordinary citizens lack the means to take part, and that NGOs may not faithfully represent them.

nature-gov-147.title: Multi-level governance: power up, down and sideways
nature-gov-147.text: Cities may produce up to 75% of global carbon dioxide emissions. National climate targets therefore depend on what towns and regions do. Multi-level governance describes this spread of power. It runs vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state bodies. Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks developed the idea in the early 1990s, studying the structures the EU built under the 1992 Maastricht Treaty. They saw authority shifting both up, from central states to bodies like the EU, and down, to regions and cities. The vertical side links higher and lower governments. The horizontal side covers cooperation between regions or municipalities. Critics say talk of "levels" implies a neat hierarchy, when real levels interact in tangled, non-hierarchical ways.

nature-gov-153.title: Spatial planning: deciding what goes where
nature-gov-153.text: Housing, industry and nature all want the same land. Spatial planning manages that contest. It makes and enforces plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed. National, regional or local governments usually do it, balancing demands from the state, the market and local communities. It spans several disciplines: land-use, urban, regional, transport and environmental planning, and maritime spatial planning at sea.

nature-gov-142.title: The law of the sea and the constitution of the oceans
nature-gov-142.text: About 64% of the world's oceans are international waters governed by the law of the sea. This body of international law sets out what states may and must do at sea, from shipping to coastal waters and seabed minerals. The modern rules began with a land grab offshore. In 1945 US President Truman claimed the natural resources of the American continental shelf. Chile, Peru and Ecuador soon claimed 200 nautical miles. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS, in force since 1994, is sometimes called the "constitution of the oceans." It gives each coastal state an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles, with sole rights to fish, minerals and seabed deposits. By June 2019, 168 states had ratified it. Non-parties such as the US still treat its rules as customary law. Bodies such as the International Seabed Authority and a tribunal in Hamburg enforce it.

nature-gov-140.title: Global environmental governance: a crowded, tangled system
nature-gov-140.text: As of 2020 the world had almost 1300 multilateral environmental agreements and over 2200 bilateral ones. Global environmental governance is the worldwide web of institutions and agreements that tackles problems crossing borders, such as climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation. A 2020 publication called it one of the most dynamic areas of world politics over the previous thirty years. Growth has brought clutter. Policy made separately by theme, sector or territory has produced treaties that overlap or clash. UNEP, the UN body that coordinates environmental responses, is widely considered weak. And some countries of the Global South see the whole effort as a "luxury" priority of the Global North that conflicts with economic development.

nature-gov-150.title: The race to the bottom
nature-gov-150.text: If one country lets factories dump untreated chemical waste, firms may move there to avoid paying for treatment. Rival countries may then loosen their own rules to keep the business. That spiral is a race to the bottom. Governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards to cut costs and attract economic activity. Ordinary competition tends to improve goods and services. This kind erodes labor laws, tax rates and environmental rules. The phrase traces to US Justice Louis Brandeis, describing states competing for corporations in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Globalization adds pressure: a producer who ignores biodiversity can undercut one who protects it. Whether the race really happens is debated. Daniel Drezner calls it a myth, and a 2022 study found no evidence of it in labor standards. Nita Rudra did find it in developing countries. Some US states even run a "race to the top," with bold environmental policies that others copy.

nature-gov-154.title: Stewardship: caring for what you hold
nature-gov-154.text: The word comes from the household steward, the keeper of the hall who looked after an owner's property. Stewardship is the ethical practice of planning and managing resources responsibly. Applied to nature, it means managing resources with an eye on quality of life for people now and in the future. Stewardship councils certify products made this way, such as the Forest Stewardship Council since 1993 and the Marine Stewardship Council since 1996.

nature-gov-158.title: The Vienna Convention: a framework to save the ozone layer
nature-gov-158.text: Research in the 1970s showed that CFCs, man-made chemicals used in refrigerators and other products, break down ozone high in the atmosphere. The 1985 Vienna Convention set the framework for cutting them worldwide. It entered into force in 1988. It set no binding cuts itself but led to the binding Montreal Protocol. Ratified by 198 states and the European Union, it is among the most universally accepted treaties ever. A Multilateral Fund has aided projects in nearly 150 countries, preventing the use of roughly 250,000 tons of ozone-destroying chemicals.

nature-gov-128.title: Local Agenda 21: sustainability at town hall
nature-gov-128.text: Chapter 28 of {{ref:nature-gov-127}} asks towns and cities to carry out its plan locally. Many did. The Rio+10 report found over 6400 local governments in 113 countries engaged in Local Agenda 21, 5120 of them in Europe. Sweden reported that 100% of its municipalities had adopted it by 2002. ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990, is widely seen as a model of how to do it.

nature-gov-121.title: The Bloomington school and the governed commons
nature-gov-121.text: One researcher at Indiana University, Ostrom, looked at pastures, fisheries and irrigation systems around the world and found something the theory said should not exist. Communities were managing shared resources well, without either the state or private owners in charge. Her 1990 book Governing the Commons challenged the tragedy of the commons, the idea that shared resources are always overused. She and Vincent Ostrom built a research tradition around such questions at the Bloomington campus. Its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, opened in 1973. The Bloomington school studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems, especially common-pool resources, decentralization and self-governance. Her work named eight design principles for lasting commons, including clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and ways to resolve conflict. In 2009 she won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it. Critics raise two doubts. Some economists question whether her findings scale up to national or global problems. Critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.

nature-gov-119.title: Fisheries co-management: sharing the helm
nature-gov-119.text: Fishers tend to ignore rules they do not understand, such as a sudden cut in the total allowable catch. Top-down fisheries management often failed for that reason. Fisheries co-management is the response: fishing communities and government share responsibility for managing aquatic resources. Five types are recognized, from government-led to user-led: instructive, consultative, cooperative, advisory and informative. Unlike pure community management, government takes part, and rules are made and enforced jointly. It blends scientific and traditional knowledge. Fishers who agree to rules are more likely to obey them and help enforce them. It is slow and costly, though. Some argue it entrenches the power of the already wealthy, while others see it as a way to empower communities.

openers.gov: Every rule about nature is really a rule about people. Governance is how societies decide what they may take from the environment, and who gets a say in those decisions: governments, businesses and ordinary citizens. Some of those decisions are written into treaties between countries, meant to bind them all. Others come from looser plans, like the action plan and the 27 principles that came out of the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. This part follows how those choices are made, and how fairly their costs and benefits are shared.
openers.environmental-governance: Nobody manages a river or a forest directly. What gets managed is people: how they fish, farm, build and dump. This chapter looks at the machinery for that, from national parks and local plans to treaties among countries and the institutions that help nations cooperate across borders. It also traces a shift in thinking, away from managing single resources and toward managing whole ecosystems, humans included, while learning from monitoring as decisions go.
